The word legend has a few distinct meanings.

The most foundational meaning of "legend" is a story from the past that has been passed down through generations — usually about a real or semi-real person, place, or event — that is widely believed but cannot be fully proven as historical fact.

Think of it this way: a legend lives somewhere between history and fiction. It's not pure fantasy, but it's not hard, documented history either. Legends usually have a grain of truth at their heart, but over time, as people retold them, details got exaggerated, romanticized, or changed.

Examples:

  • The legend of King Arthur — a king who may have existed in some form, but the stories of Excalibur, Merlin, and the Round Table are layered with myth.
  • The legend of Robin Hood — a figure who stole from the rich and gave to the poor. There may have been a real person like him, but the full story is almost certainly embellished.
  • The legend of William Tell — a Swiss hero who supposedly shot an apple off his son's head. Widely celebrated, but historians debate whether he truly existed.

Legends typically celebrate heroic deeds, extraordinary courage, or remarkable events. They are culturally important — they carry the values, fears, and ideals of the people who tell them. A society's legends reveal what that society considers admirable or meaningful.

How "legend" differs from similar words:

It helps to understand what a legend is not, because learners often confuse these:

  • A myth is a story primarily about gods, divine beings, or supernatural forces, and usually explains the origin of the world or natural phenomena. (The Greek story of how Prometheus stole fire from the gods is a myth.)
  • A legend is primarily about humans — often historical or heroic figures — set in the real world, with events that could have happened, even if they probably didn't happen exactly as described.
  • A fable is a short, clearly fictional story (often with talking animals) designed to teach a moral lesson. (Aesop's fables.)
  • A fairy tale is an imaginative, clearly fictional story meant for entertainment, often involving magic, kingdoms, and heroes. Nobody believes Cinderella actually happened.
  • Folklore is a broader umbrella term for the traditional stories, beliefs, customs, and oral traditions of a community — legends are a part of folklore.

So the key qualities of a legend are: human characters, a historical or real-world setting, a story passed down over generations, cultural significance, and uncertain truth.
Meaning 2: A Remarkably Famous or Admired Person

In modern use — especially in spoken and informal English — "legend" is used to describe a person who is extraordinarily famous, admired, or skilled in a particular field, to the point where they feel almost larger than life.

This meaning flows naturally from the first: a legend in the story sense is a larger-than-life figure celebrated across time. When you call a living (or recently deceased) person a legend, you are saying they have reached that same level of greatness — their story will be told for generations.

Examples:

  • "Sachin Tendulkar is a cricket legend." (He achieved so much that his name will always be spoken in the same breath as the sport.)
  • "Muhammad Ali was a boxing legend."
  • "She's a legend in the fashion world."

Notice the phrase "a legend in [field]" — this is a very common and natural construction.

You can also use "legend" on its own as a direct noun:

  • "He is a legend."
  • "She became a legend."

Colloquial/informal use: In British and Australian English especially, people casually call someone a "legend" to simply mean they did something impressive, kind, or helpful:

  • "You fixed my computer? You're an absolute legend!"

In this informal use, it's a strong compliment but not literally claiming the person is historically famous. Context makes this clear.
Meaning 3: The Explanatory Key on a Map or Diagram

This meaning is more technical. On a map, chart, graph, or diagram, the legend is the box or section that explains what the symbols, colors, lines, or patterns in the image mean.

Think of any map you've seen. There's usually a small area on the side or corner that says something like:

  • Blue shading = ocean
  • Green area = forest
  • Red line = national border
  • Star symbol = capital city
  • Dotted line = railway

That explanatory section is called the legend (also sometimes called a key). Without it, you can't properly read or interpret the map.

The same applies to charts and graphs:

  • On a bar chart comparing sales across three products, the legend tells you which color bar represents which product.
  • On a scientific diagram, the legend explains what each label or symbol stands for.

Examples in sentences:

  • "Refer to the legend on the bottom-left of the map to understand the color coding."
  • "The legend shows that the red line represents temperature and the blue line represents rainfall."

This is a more specialized and less commonly used meaning. A legend can refer to the words or text inscribed (written or engraved) on a coin, medal, seal, monument, or coat of arms.

For example:

  • The words around the edge of a coin are its legend.
  • The text on a commemorative medal, engraved beneath an image, is its legend.

You'll mostly encounter this meaning in formal, historical, or numismatic (coin-related) writing.

It's worth noting that these meanings are not random — they share a common thread:

A legend is always something that records, communicates, or celebrates something significant — whether it's a story that preserves cultural memory, a person whose greatness deserves to be remembered, the explanatory text that makes information readable, or an inscription that marks an important object.

The word carries the idea of something noteworthy being put into words for others to understand and remember.

ContextCorrect Use
  • Talking about a traditional story → "the legend of [name/place]"
  • Describing a famously great person → "[person] is a legend" / "a legend of [field]"
  • Referring to a map or chart key → "see the legend" / "according to the legend"
  • Referring to an inscription → "the legend on the coin reads..."

The word carries weight and respect. Calling someone a legend — even informally — is a genuine compliment. And a story being called a legend implies it has stood the test of time and carries real cultural value. It's not a small word.
